foundations.title: Professional Foundations — New York
foundations.action: Confirm the licence, current registration, scope and supervision required for the actual work.
foundations.record: Explain the professional role, service purpose and confidentiality limits. Check any additional designation or qualification required for a statutory mental-health function. Use supervision and continuing education to improve the effect of practice, including cultural responsiveness and access. The Office of the Professions addresses professional regulation; benefit decisions, agency services and mental-health detention have different complaint or review routes. Explain which body can address the person’s concern and desired remedy.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — New York
care-support.action: Identify Medicaid eligibility, the service requested and the responsible assessment and authorisation bodies.
care-support.record: Obtain the applicable community assessment and practitioner information through the current NYIAP process. Confirm the plan of care, amount, duration, frequency and actual provider arrangements. Record voluntary informal support, unmet needs and the notice, plan appeal or fair-hearing route for a disputed decision. Managed-care appeals and state fair hearings depend on the decision and programme. Read the notice for time limits, any required internal step and continued-benefit rules. A complaint to the provider is different from challenging the authorisation.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — New York
mca.action: Specify the decision, support the person and identify the applicable healthcare or guardianship framework.
mca.record: Check any proxy, prior decision or court order and the scope of authority. Where FHCDA applies, use the statutory surrogate priority, eligibility and decision standards. For an Article 81 issue, document functional evidence, likely harm and less restrictive available resources. The FHCDA includes requirements for surrogate decisions, with additional safeguards for life-sustaining treatment. Article 81 has court procedures and tailored powers. Disagreement about a healthcare choice should not automatically become a request for broad guardianship.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — New York
dols.action: Describe the restriction, setting, person’s wishes and current legal status.
dols.record: Read the actual Article 9 documents or Article 81 order and identify its limits. Check separate authority and safeguards for restraint or treatment. Arrange Mental Hygiene Legal Service or other appropriate legal support and the relevant court or complaint process. A court challenge to detention, review of guardianship powers and a service complaint address different matters. Explain the route relevant to the actual restriction. The person should have accessible rights information and help to express and act on objections.

mha.title: Mental Health — New York
mha.action: Identify the exact Article 9 route and evidence for its current criteria.
mha.record: Check the authorised practitioner, examinations, forms, notices and timing. Use the current OMH guidance, including the updated essential-needs wording, and consider voluntary alternatives. Separate detention from treatment authority and coordinate accepted discharge and community-support arrangements. Section 9.39 requires rights notice and provides a court-hearing route, with Mental Hygiene Legal Service involvement. Different statuses have different review procedures. A treatment-over-objection issue needs its own analysis and should not be assumed resolved by admission.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — New York
safeguarding.action: Identify the harm, functional difficulties and whether responsible assistance is actually available.
safeguarding.record: Refer through the appropriate local adult-protective services route and address immediate danger. Check any separate provider, facility, police or mandated-reporting requirement. Use the least restrictive appropriate response and distinguish voluntary services from court-authorised measures. The adult’s agreement and participation remain important; an APS referral does not confer general authority to force services. Where a court measure is proposed, identify its own conditions and representation. Explain the local service complaint and relevant legal route.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — New York
children.action: Identify the reporter role, child’s age, alleged responsible person and facts supporting reasonable cause.
children.record: Use the required SCR reporting process and immediate emergency response where necessary. Complete the applicable written follow-up and document receipt, facts and safety actions. Consider police, institutional or other reporting duties separately and coordinate family support. Explain the child-protective process and access to support or legal advice. Reporting is not a court determination of abuse or authority for every intervention. Preserve the child’s account and the distinction between an allegation, investigation and finding.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — New York
rights.action: Identify the organisation, record and state or federal privacy provisions involved.
rights.record: Arrange accessible communication, interpretation and culturally responsive participation. Check the legal basis, purpose and scope of disclosure, including any special rules for proceedings. Explain records access, correction, complaints and the applicable patient-rights or legal review route. A privacy complaint, professional complaint and mental-hygiene rights challenge address different questions. A request from police, a lawyer or another service does not itself establish authority to release a whole record. Obtain the relevant advice and document the decision.

sources.title: New York Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: New York Education Law and the Office of the Professions distinguish Licensed Master Social Workers (LMSWs) from Licensed Clinical Social Workers (LCSWs). An LMSW may provide clinical social-work services, including diagnosis, psychotherapy and assessment-based treatment planning, only under the required supervision; an LCSW may provide those services independently within competence.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Licensure, registration, a permitted practice setting and any separate mental-hygiene designation must be checked. Employer seniority does not create a statutory power. Professional ethical guidance should be read alongside state law and applicable agency obligations.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Confirm the licence, current registration, scope and supervision required for the actual work. Explain the professional role, service purpose and confidentiality limits. Check any additional designation or qualification required for a statutory mental-health function. Use supervision and continuing education to improve the effect of practice, including cultural responsiveness and access.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Office of the Professions addresses professional regulation; benefit decisions, agency services and mental-health detention have different complaint or review routes. Explain which body can address the person’s concern and desired remedy.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating LMSW and LCSW practice permissions as interchangeable.

flashcardDecks.title: Social Care and Support — New York

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Medicaid personal care and Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Services involve assessment, medical necessity and service authorisation. The New York Independent Assessor Program (NYIAP), local departments of social services and managed-care organisations have different responsibilities. An assessment does not itself authorise every requested hour of care.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Current Department of Health guidance includes minimum-needs requirements introduced in 2025 and legacy-status arrangements. Check the person’s programme and circumstances before applying a new rule or assuming that an existing recipient follows the same route as a new applicant.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify Medicaid eligibility, the service requested and the responsible assessment and authorisation bodies. Obtain the applicable community assessment and practitioner information through the current NYIAP process. Confirm the plan of care, amount, duration, frequency and actual provider arrangements. Record voluntary informal support, unmet needs and the notice, plan appeal or fair-hearing route for a disputed decision.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Managed-care appeals and state fair hearings depend on the decision and programme. Read the notice for time limits, any required internal step and continued-benefit rules. A complaint to the provider is different from challenging the authorisation.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing NYIAP assessment with final service authorisation or overlooking current minimum-needs and legacy rules.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Healthcare proxies, the Family Health Care Decisions Act (FHCDA) and Mental Hygiene Law Article 81 guardianship are distinct. Check the healthcare setting and statutory scope before using the FHCDA surrogate list. A healthcare proxy or a valid patient decision may need consideration before a default surrogate route. FHCDA capacity concerns understanding and appreciating what the proposed care involves and its consequences, including risks, benefits and alternatives, and making an informed choice. Use the statutory assessment process; a social-work opinion alone does not replace a required practitioner determination.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Article 81 requires a necessity assessment and, where incapacity is alleged, clear and convincing evidence about inability to meet personal or property needs and insufficient understanding and appreciation of that inability, with likely harm. The court should tailor powers and consider available alternatives. A diagnosis alone does not establish the guardianship test.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Specify the decision, support the person and identify the applicable healthcare or guardianship framework. Check any proxy, prior decision or court order and the scope of authority. Where FHCDA applies, use the statutory surrogate priority, eligibility and decision standards. For an Article 81 issue, document functional evidence, likely harm and less restrictive available resources.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The FHCDA includes requirements for surrogate decisions, with additional safeguards for life-sustaining treatment. Article 81 has court procedures and tailored powers. Disagreement about a healthcare choice should not automatically become a request for broad guardianship.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating family status as priority over every valid appointment or using diagnosis alone to establish Article 81 incapacity.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Mental Hygiene Law Article 9 admission, Article 81 guardianship and facility restraint rules concern different authorities. An Article 81 guardian receives only the powers granted by the court. The personal-needs provisions do not make guardianship a general permission for involuntary psychiatric admission.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Separate a placement decision, the actual restriction on departure and the authority for treatment. An institution should identify the legal basis for each measure and the required review. A family’s agreement or an administrative discharge concern does not establish detention authority.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe the restriction, setting, person’s wishes and current legal status. Read the actual Article 9 documents or Article 81 order and identify its limits. Check separate authority and safeguards for restraint or treatment. Arrange Mental Hygiene Legal Service or other appropriate legal support and the relevant court or complaint process.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A court challenge to detention, review of guardianship powers and a service complaint address different matters. Explain the route relevant to the actual restriction. The person should have accessible rights information and help to express and act on objections.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating a guardian’s placement power as a universal psychiatric detention power.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Mental Hygiene Law Article 9 provides distinct voluntary, emergency and other involuntary-admission routes. Section 9.39 concerns immediate hospital observation, care and treatment where the mental-illness and likely-serious-harm conditions are met. Its current definition includes specified inability or refusal, because of mental illness, to meet essential needs causing substantial risk of physical harm.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Under this route, retention beyond 48 hours requires confirmation by another physician from the psychiatric staff; the emergency period is limited to 15 days. Further retention requires the applicable additional process. These are route-specific limits, not rules to apply indiscriminately to every Article 9 admission.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the exact Article 9 route and evidence for its current criteria. Check the authorised practitioner, examinations, forms, notices and timing. Use the current OMH guidance, including the updated essential-needs wording, and consider voluntary alternatives. Separate detention from treatment authority and coordinate accepted discharge and community-support arrangements.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Section 9.39 requires rights notice and provides a court-hearing route, with Mental Hygiene Legal Service involvement. Different statuses have different review procedures. A treatment-over-objection issue needs its own analysis and should not be assumed resolved by admission.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using an outdated threat-only account of serious harm or confusing the time limits of different admission routes.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Social Services Law section 473 provides protective services for adults meeting its conditions, without regard to income. The framework concerns mental or physical impairments affecting ability to manage resources, daily living or protection from harm, together with the absence of someone available, willing and able to assist responsibly.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Local social-services districts provide adult-protective services and coordinate with health, mental-health, legal and other agencies. A general APS referral, a setting-specific mandated report and an application for guardianship are different matters. Do not invent a universal adult-reporting duty from the child-reporting rules.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the harm, functional difficulties and whether responsible assistance is actually available. Refer through the appropriate local adult-protective services route and address immediate danger. Check any separate provider, facility, police or mandated-reporting requirement. Use the least restrictive appropriate response and distinguish voluntary services from court-authorised measures.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The adult’s agreement and participation remain important; an APS referral does not confer general authority to force services. Where a court measure is proposed, identify its own conditions and representation. Explain the local service complaint and relevant legal route.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming that any listed relative rules out APS support or that a referral automatically authorises guardianship.

flashcardDecks.title: Children, Families and Transitions — New York

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Social Services Law sections 413 and 415 identify mandated reporters and reporting procedures. Covered social workers must act on reasonable cause to suspect abuse or maltreatment within the statutory circumstances. The Statewide Central Register route has defined scope, including the relationship of the alleged responsible person to the child.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An immediate report and the required written follow-up are distinct steps; section 415 generally requires the written report within 48 hours. Abuse by someone outside the child-protective reporting definition may still require police or another safety response. Do not treat an out-of-scope SCR decision as proof that no action is needed.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the reporter role, child’s age, alleged responsible person and facts supporting reasonable cause. Use the required SCR reporting process and immediate emergency response where necessary. Complete the applicable written follow-up and document receipt, facts and safety actions. Consider police, institutional or other reporting duties separately and coordinate family support.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the child-protective process and access to support or legal advice. Reporting is not a court determination of abuse or authority for every intervention. Preserve the child’s account and the distinction between an allegation, investigation and finding.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing reasonable cause with proof, or assuming the SCR is the only possible route for every threat to a child.

flashcardDecks.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — New York

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New York practice guide?
cards.answer: Federal civil-rights and disability law, New York Human Rights Law and sector-specific patient rights apply according to the service and decision. Identify the responsible body and the actual access barrier or restriction rather than assuming every complaint uses the same route.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: HIPAA applies to covered entities and business associates; Mental Hygiene Law section 33.13 protects covered clinical records, and Part 2 provides additional requirements for certain substance-use-disorder records. The 2024 Part 2 changes required compliance by February 2026. Determine which overlapping rules apply before sharing.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the organisation, record and state or federal privacy provisions involved. Arrange accessible communication, interpretation and culturally responsive participation. Check the legal basis, purpose and scope of disclosure, including any special rules for proceedings. Explain records access, correction, complaints and the applicable patient-rights or legal review route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A privacy complaint, professional complaint and mental-hygiene rights challenge address different questions. A request from police, a lawyer or another service does not itself establish authority to release a whole record. Obtain the relevant advice and document the decision.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Checking HIPAA while overlooking state mental-hygiene or specially protected substance-use records.

glossaryTerms.term: New York State Education Department, Office of the Professions
glossaryTerms.definition: The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An LMSW is offered an independent psychotherapy caseload without the supervision required for clinical work.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the scope, setting and supervision requirements before accepting the arrangement. Arrange appropriate oversight or a lawful alternative and explain the practitioner’s status accurately. A social-work licence does not mean that both licence categories have identical clinical authority.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person receives an assessment but the plan authorises fewer hours than requested, assuming a relative will provide the rest.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the assessment evidence, the relative’s voluntarily offered assistance and the plan’s written reasons. Identify the appropriate appeal or hearing process and interim safety arrangements. Do not treat an assumed family contribution as available care.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A patient’s adult child assumes they can decide because of family status, while a healthcare proxy names a close friend.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the patient’s own decision-making ability and check the proxy’s operation and scope. Do not jump to the default surrogate list. If a separate guardianship concern exists, identify its functional evidence and alternatives rather than using it to bypass the healthcare arrangement.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A facility says a guardian’s authority to choose residence allows it to admit the adult involuntarily to a psychiatric hospital.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Read the order and Article 81 limits, then identify whether Article 9 criteria and procedures are met. Obtain appropriate legal and clinical advice and consider voluntary alternatives. Residence powers should not be used as a substitute for psychiatric admission safeguards.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A team assumes emergency admission requires an express threat and ignores evidence that mental illness prevents a person obtaining essential medical care.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Apply the current statutory definition and assess the connection to substantial physical harm, rather than relying on a threat-only summary. Consider realistic support and alternatives, record each criterion and explain the person’s rights and review route.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult cannot obtain food or manage money because of impairment, and the only relative listed as a contact is unwilling to assist.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the actual availability and reliability of help against the protective-service conditions. Arrange immediate practical support and the appropriate APS response. A name on a contact form is not evidence that someone can responsibly meet the need.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A social worker hears a disclosure but is told to wait for a manager to decide whether it is sufficiently certain to report.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess reasonable cause under the statute and act through the required procedure. Record the relationship and facts that determine the correct recipient. Do not require certainty or delay a required report for an internal meeting.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — New York
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A mental-health service receives a broad request for records and assumes HIPAA permission alone resolves all confidentiality requirements.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the record’s coverage under state mental-hygiene law and any Part 2 restrictions as well as HIPAA. Identify the actual request and lawful basis, limit disclosure and explain the person’s rights where appropriate. One applicable rule does not remove another.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
New York Education Law and the Office of the Professions distinguish Licensed Master Social Workers (LMSWs) from Licensed Clinical Social Workers (LCSWs). An LMSW may provide clinical social-work services, including diagnosis, psychotherapy and assessment-based treatment planning, only under the required supervision; an LCSW may provide those services independently within competence.

Licensure, registration, a permitted practice setting and any separate mental-hygiene designation must be checked. Employer seniority does not create a statutory power. Professional ethical guidance should be read alongside state law and applicable agency obligations.

Local pathway:
Confirm the licence, current registration, scope and supervision required for the actual work.
Explain the professional role, service purpose and confidentiality limits.
Check any additional designation or qualification required for a statutory mental-health function.
Use supervision and continuing education to improve the effect of practice, including cultural responsiveness and access.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Office of the Professions addresses professional regulation; benefit decisions, agency services and mental-health detention have different complaint or review routes. Explain which body can address the person’s concern and desired remedy.

Sources:
https://www.op.nysed.gov/professions/social-work/faqs/what-difference-between-lmsw-and-lcsw
https://www.op.nysed.gov/professions/licensed-master-social-worker/laws-rules-regulations

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Medicaid personal care and Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Services involve assessment, medical necessity and service authorisation. The New York Independent Assessor Program (NYIAP), local departments of social services and managed-care organisations have different responsibilities. An assessment does not itself authorise every requested hour of care.

Current Department of Health guidance includes minimum-needs requirements introduced in 2025 and legacy-status arrangements. Check the person’s programme and circumstances before applying a new rule or assuming that an existing recipient follows the same route as a new applicant.

Local pathway:
Identify Medicaid eligibility, the service requested and the responsible assessment and authorisation bodies.
Obtain the applicable community assessment and practitioner information through the current NYIAP process.
Confirm the plan of care, amount, duration, frequency and actual provider arrangements.
Record voluntary informal support, unmet needs and the notice, plan appeal or fair-hearing route for a disputed decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Managed-care appeals and state fair hearings depend on the decision and programme. Read the notice for time limits, any required internal step and continued-benefit rules. A complaint to the provider is different from challenging the authorisation.

Sources:
https://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/medicaid/redesign/nyiap/ldss-mmco.htm
https://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/medicaid/redesign/nyiap/repository/index.htm
https://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/managed_care/plans/min_needs.htm

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Healthcare proxies, the Family Health Care Decisions Act (FHCDA) and Mental Hygiene Law Article 81 guardianship are distinct. Check the healthcare setting and statutory scope before using the FHCDA surrogate list. A healthcare proxy or a valid patient decision may need consideration before a default surrogate route. FHCDA capacity concerns understanding and appreciating what the proposed care involves and its consequences, including risks, benefits and alternatives, and making an informed choice. Use the statutory assessment process; a social-work opinion alone does not replace a required practitioner determination.

Article 81 requires a necessity assessment and, where incapacity is alleged, clear and convincing evidence about inability to meet personal or property needs and insufficient understanding and appreciation of that inability, with likely harm. The court should tailor powers and consider available alternatives. A diagnosis alone does not establish the guardianship test.

Local pathway:
Specify the decision, support the person and identify the applicable healthcare or guardianship framework.
Check any proxy, prior decision or court order and the scope of authority.
Where FHCDA applies, use the statutory surrogate priority, eligibility and decision standards.
For an Article 81 issue, document functional evidence, likely harm and less restrictive available resources.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The FHCDA includes requirements for surrogate decisions, with additional safeguards for life-sustaining treatment. Article 81 has court procedures and tailored powers. Disagreement about a healthcare choice should not automatically become a request for broad guardianship.

Sources:
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBH/2994-D
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/MHY/81.02
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBH/A29-C
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBH/2994-A

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Mental Hygiene Law Article 9 admission, Article 81 guardianship and facility restraint rules concern different authorities. An Article 81 guardian receives only the powers granted by the court. The personal-needs provisions do not make guardianship a general permission for involuntary psychiatric admission.

Separate a placement decision, the actual restriction on departure and the authority for treatment. An institution should identify the legal basis for each measure and the required review. A family’s agreement or an administrative discharge concern does not establish detention authority.

Local pathway:
Describe the restriction, setting, person’s wishes and current legal status.
Read the actual Article 9 documents or Article 81 order and identify its limits.
Check separate authority and safeguards for restraint or treatment.
Arrange Mental Hygiene Legal Service or other appropriate legal support and the relevant court or complaint process.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A court challenge to detention, review of guardianship powers and a service complaint address different matters. Explain the route relevant to the actual restriction. The person should have accessible rights information and help to express and act on objections.

Sources:
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/MHY/81.22
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/MHY/9.39
https://omh.ny.gov/omhweb/guidance/transport-civil-voluntary-involuntary-admissions-statutes.html

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Mental Hygiene Law Article 9 provides distinct voluntary, emergency and other involuntary-admission routes. Section 9.39 concerns immediate hospital observation, care and treatment where the mental-illness and likely-serious-harm conditions are met. Its current definition includes specified inability or refusal, because of mental illness, to meet essential needs causing substantial risk of physical harm.

Under this route, retention beyond 48 hours requires confirmation by another physician from the psychiatric staff; the emergency period is limited to 15 days. Further retention requires the applicable additional process. These are route-specific limits, not rules to apply indiscriminately to every Article 9 admission.

Local pathway:
Identify the exact Article 9 route and evidence for its current criteria.
Check the authorised practitioner, examinations, forms, notices and timing.
Use the current OMH guidance, including the updated essential-needs wording, and consider voluntary alternatives.
Separate detention from treatment authority and coordinate accepted discharge and community-support arrangements.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Section 9.39 requires rights notice and provides a court-hearing route, with Mental Hygiene Legal Service involvement. Different statuses have different review procedures. A treatment-over-objection issue needs its own analysis and should not be assumed resolved by admission.

Sources:
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/MHY/9.39
https://omh.ny.gov/omhweb/guidance/transport-civil-voluntary-involuntary-admissions-statutes.html
https://omh.ny.gov/omhweb/guidance/

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Social Services Law section 473 provides protective services for adults meeting its conditions, without regard to income. The framework concerns mental or physical impairments affecting ability to manage resources, daily living or protection from harm, together with the absence of someone available, willing and able to assist responsibly.

Local social-services districts provide adult-protective services and coordinate with health, mental-health, legal and other agencies. A general APS referral, a setting-specific mandated report and an application for guardianship are different matters. Do not invent a universal adult-reporting duty from the child-reporting rules.

Local pathway:
Identify the harm, functional difficulties and whether responsible assistance is actually available.
Refer through the appropriate local adult-protective services route and address immediate danger.
Check any separate provider, facility, police or mandated-reporting requirement.
Use the least restrictive appropriate response and distinguish voluntary services from court-authorised measures.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The adult’s agreement and participation remain important; an APS referral does not confer general authority to force services. Where a court measure is proposed, identify its own conditions and representation. Explain the local service complaint and relevant legal route.

Sources:
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/SOS/473
https://ocfs.ny.gov/programs/adult-svcs/

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Social Services Law sections 413 and 415 identify mandated reporters and reporting procedures. Covered social workers must act on reasonable cause to suspect abuse or maltreatment within the statutory circumstances. The Statewide Central Register route has defined scope, including the relationship of the alleged responsible person to the child.

An immediate report and the required written follow-up are distinct steps; section 415 generally requires the written report within 48 hours. Abuse by someone outside the child-protective reporting definition may still require police or another safety response. Do not treat an out-of-scope SCR decision as proof that no action is needed.

Local pathway:
Identify the reporter role, child’s age, alleged responsible person and facts supporting reasonable cause.
Use the required SCR reporting process and immediate emergency response where necessary.
Complete the applicable written follow-up and document receipt, facts and safety actions.
Consider police, institutional or other reporting duties separately and coordinate family support.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the child-protective process and access to support or legal advice. Reporting is not a court determination of abuse or authority for every intervention. Preserve the child’s account and the distinction between an allegation, investigation and finding.

Sources:
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/SOS/413
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/SOS/415
https://ocfs.ny.gov/programs/cps/

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
New York practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Federal civil-rights and disability law, New York Human Rights Law and sector-specific patient rights apply according to the service and decision. Identify the responsible body and the actual access barrier or restriction rather than assuming every complaint uses the same route.

HIPAA applies to covered entities and business associates; Mental Hygiene Law section 33.13 protects covered clinical records, and Part 2 provides additional requirements for certain substance-use-disorder records. The 2024 Part 2 changes required compliance by February 2026. Determine which overlapping rules apply before sharing.

Local pathway:
Identify the organisation, record and state or federal privacy provisions involved.
Arrange accessible communication, interpretation and culturally responsive participation.
Check the legal basis, purpose and scope of disclosure, including any special rules for proceedings.
Explain records access, correction, complaints and the applicable patient-rights or legal review route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A privacy complaint, professional complaint and mental-hygiene rights challenge address different questions. A request from police, a lawyer or another service does not itself establish authority to release a whole record. Obtain the relevant advice and document the decision.

Sources:
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/MHY/33.13
https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/mental-health/index.html
https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/part-2/index.html
